div.p: Computational chemistry tools are widely used to study the behaviour of chemical phenomena. Yet, the complexity of these tools can make them inaccessible to non-specialists and challenging even for experts. In this work, we introduce El Agente Q, an LLM-based multi-agent system that dynamically generates and executes quantum chemistry workflows from natural language user prompts. The system is built on a novel cognitive architecture featuring a hierarchical memory framework that enables flexible task decomposition, adaptive tool selection, post-analysis, and autonomous file handling and submission. El Agente Q is benchmarked on six university-level course exercises and two case studies, demonstrating robust problem-solving performance (averaging >87% task success) and adaptive error handling through in situ debugging. It also supports longer-term, multi-step task execution for more complex workflows, while maintaining transparency through detailed action trace logs. Together, these capabilities lay the foundation for increasingly autonomous and accessible quantum chemistry.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computational chemistry is an essential tool in modern chemical research, allowing scientists to systematically study diverse molecular systems, properties, and mechanisms (1; 2; 3; 4; 5). Simulation streamlines the design of new drugs, catalysts, and materials by efficiently screening target molecules and reducing experimental workload (6; 7; 8; 9; 10; 11; 12). In principle, simulation is also accessible to anyone with access to a computer. Despite these advantages, computational chemistry software has long been known for its steep learning curve. Users must possess expert knowledge to navigate a vast array of tools, configure input parameters, and interpret results accurately. Additionally, handling computational divergences, runtime errors, and other technical challenges demands significant expertise, making the field less accessible to non-specialists.

Moreover, these runtime errors can be challenging to understand even for experienced users and thus require considerable time for troubleshooting calculations rather than focusing on scientific discovery. While integrated workflows (13; 14; 15; 16; 17; 18; 19; 20; 21) and advanced interactive control (22; 23; 24; 25; 26) can alleviate some of these challenges, they come with limitations of their own. These pipelines often rely on a fixed set of tools and predefined workflows, which can be cumbersome when adapting to new problems or specific research needs. For example, while calculating the ring strain of cycloalkanes involves a series of routine computational chemistry protocols, like geometry generation, optimization, and obtaining appropriate energetic differences, to our knowledge, there is no computational workflow specifically designed to calculate the ring strain of cycloalkanes. Although modern workflow packages allow for adding such functionality, these workflows must be implemented by experts, which makes scaling difficult for the diverse number of workflows a chemist might need. Furthermore, a rigid workflow structure cannot generalize to complex cases that require domain-specific chemical intuition in more advanced tasks. As a result, despite automation, such pipelines may still fall short in facilitating truly accessible and adaptable computational chemistry workflows.

Large language models (LLMs) can be part of a potential solution to these problems (27; 28; 29; 30; 31; 32). Through pre-training, LLMs not only encode chemistry knowledge in their training data (33; 34; 35; 36), which is often derived from scientific literature and textbooks (37), but also gain the ability to interpret and generalize human expertise stored in textual formats via in-context learning (38; 39; 40). This capability enables the transfer of chemistry knowledge from experts to LLM-based systems through natural language descriptions (41; 42). For instance, Jacobs and Pollice (32) recently demonstrated how an LLM can be fine-tuned to emit complete ORCA input files in a single pass. Furthermore, recent advancements in LLM-based agents allow LLMs to execute code and experiments based on this knowledge (43). Various frameworks have been developed to enhance these agents with tools, memory, and human communication interfaces (44; 45; 46; 47; 48; 49). LLM-based agents have shown promising results in retrieving chemistry knowledge, designing and conducting experiments, and analyzing results (50; 51; 52). However, existing approaches remain limited, often relying on a small set of tools and relatively simple experimental or computational setups. This limitation stems in part from the significant human effort required to develop and validate tools, as well as the challenge of selecting the appropriate tool from a large tool set. A key challenge, therefore, is scaling these agent systems while minimizing the human effort needed to transfer and apply their knowledge effectively.

In this work, we introduce El Agente,foot_0 a novel cognitive architecture for language agents, and apply it to automate complex computational and quantum chemistry tasks. We refer to this application of El Agente as El Agente Q (Figure 1). El Agente employs a hierarchical network of specialized LLM-based agents, each equipped with an extensive list of available tools. This hierarchy effectively filters out the irrelevant context for each agent, significantly enhancing the decision-making performance of the entire system, enabling complex planning and task execution via feedback loops. To minimize the human effort required for knowledge transfer, we developed multiple interfaces allowing human experts to inject knowledge into the system through both programming and natural language conversation. El Agente Q is part of a broader trajectory of agentic systems in computational chemistry. Early rule-based agents were used for modelling self-assembly (53; 54). More recently, agent-based systems have evolved to incorporate knowledge graphs as structured data backends, enabling more semantic and interconnected workflows (55; 56; 57; 58). Entering the LLM era, a new generation of agents has emerged across a broad Figure 1 Schematic overview of El Agente Q, an LLM-based multi-agent system for automated planning, scheduling, execution, and troubleshooting computational chemistry tasks. The hierarchical design allows the top-level agent (the computational chemist) to focus on high-level planning. Meanwhile, lower-level agents (e.g., the geometry optimization module) specialize in executing their allotted tasks in the action space, calling software for action execution, or accessing databases for information storage. The agent's chatbox interface facilitates human-agent interaction through natural language.

range of scientific tasks (59; 60; 61; 62; 63; 64; 65; 66; 67). For a comprehensive overview of these LLM-based agentic systems, we refer the reader to Ref. (43). Specific applications of LLM-based agents in computational chemistry include MDCrow (68) for molecular dynamics, and AutoSolvateWeb (69) for solvated molecules. Our work builds on this growing landscape by focusing on a multi-agent system capable of simultaneously coordinating several computational chemistry tasks. Unlike previous works, El Agente Q introduces key features such as automated error recovery, shell-level interaction, and action trace exports. Notably, it utilizes LLMs to dynamically route tasks and tools, providing flexibility and adaptability that traditional workflow management systems struggle to achieve. and the limitations and challenges to be addressed.

div.head: System architecture: El Agente
div.p: El Agente is the novel cognitive architecture, which we used as the foundation to develop El Agente Q. El Agente was designed to improve the agents' planning, reasoning, and long-term acting capability. It integrates a working memory, a long-term memory, and an LLM-based reasoning core, following the CoALA agent design framework (75) and the Soar architecture (76; 77). Specifically, our implementation transforms and extends the original CoALA architecture into a hierarchical cybernetic agentic network to enable hierarchical planning, long-term memory retrieval, and modular memory management. The working memory is updated through four components: (i) the global memory, which maintains shared context across all agents; (ii) an agent-specific conversation history, which tracks local decision-making and interactions; (iii) a grounding mechanism, which brings in environment information such as file directory tree structure to allow the agent to perceive the working environment; and (iv) a long-term memory, which is composed of procedural, semantic, and episodic memory, to define the expert agent's behaviour (Figure 2). The LLM reasoning core then utilizes the specialized working memory to plan, reason, act, critique, and report task execution in real time, enabling flexible, dynamic synthesis and execution of complex, multi-step workflows.

In particular, the procedural memory is represented as a hierarchical multi-agent team working in a cybernetic network fashion to generate procedures dynamically (Figure 2-iv). Within the hierarchical team, each agent (a node in the procedural memory) is equipped with four components: (i) a specialized context that defines its role and job scope, and contains domain-specific knowledge, (ii) its own semantic memory, which stores role-specific patterns and decision rules that can be dynamically retrieved, enabling consistent expert-like reasoning, (iii) a set of callable modules (i.e. connections between nodes) that enable the agent to either interface directly with available tools for task execution or delegate subtasks to other agents, allowing for dynamic task decomposition and routing across the network. The callable modules follow common procedural task decomposition logic to organize the agents into a hierarchical team. The last component (iv) is the agent's individual episodic memory that captures prior decisions and results. However, episodic memory is not activated in our current implementation of El Agente Q.

Figure 2 A high-level view of the cognitive architecture of El Agente, where the working memory is composed of (i) a global memory, (ii) an agent-specific conversation history, (iii) a grounding mechanism, and (iv) retrieved long-term memory, all of which go into the LLM reasoning core. The long-term memory is composed of procedural, semantic, and episodic memory. The procedural memory itself is a procedural memory network consisting of a network structure and a procedural memory node. Each procedural memory node makes the reasoning core aware of its current role, semantic memory, episodic memory, and allowable action space, which are processed as part of the working memory. Note that in El Agente Q, the episodic memory has been disabled.

Throughout a session, El Agente Q records its action trace. The system can export this trace to a Jupyter notebook, where the tools invoked by the agents are converted into native Python functions. This functionality allows users to review the steps taken by the agents to complete a task. This feature is particularly useful for human experts to verify the correctness of the procedure. Crucially, users can also adapt these notebooks into standardized workflow pipelines for high-throughput virtual screening.

div.head: Implementation of El Agente for quantum chemistry tasks: El Agente Q
div.p: El Agente Q (Figure 3) features the computational chemist agent as the top-level agent for high-level planning based on the user's task prompt. The computational chemist is assisted by mid-level agents, which can be broadly categorized into three functional modules based on overarching job scope. These modules are analogous to a company's departments, in the sense that they have well-defined functions that contribute to the overall function of a complex system. These modules are (i) the geometry module, which manages tasks like molecular structure construction and geometry optimization, (ii) the quantum calculation module, which performs all calculation-related tasks such as preparing and running executable input files and debugging output files, and (iii) the file I/O module, which manages file system operations such as reading and extracting properties from output files, as well as job submission.

Each agent determines its next callable module based on its domain-specific knowledge. These modules include tool selection and task delegation logic (e.g., when to use RDKit versus OpenBabel for the geometry generation agent), expert-recommended typical action sequences (e.g., geometry optimization → frequency analysis), expected input and output file formats, common output handling heuristics (e.g., detecting and resolving imaginary frequencies after optimization), and subtask delegation. For example, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are managed by the DFT agent, which can call the input file expert to generate ORCA input files, and the SLURM agent to submit ORCA calculations.

Within such a hierarchical planning framework, higher-level agents only handle broad strategic planning, directing low-level agents to manage execution details, who respond with summarized feedback. For example, when instructed to perform a DFT calculation, the DFT agent only generates high-level subtasks such as generating input files, organizing job folders, and submitting calculations. Lower-level implementation detailssuch as deciding the keywords and blocks required for ORCA input file creation, writing the Python command to execute the file organization, and interfacing with the HPC server -are delegated to one of the following agents: the ORCA input file expert, the file I/O agent, and the ORCA runner agent. Similarly, these individual agents only provide concise, high-level feedback to the DFT agent without overwhelming the higher-level agent with implementation specifics. This Markov-style thinking process effectively reduces the planning complexity to improve instruction adherence, enhances local problem-solving ability, and shortens the active context for individual agents, which allows El Agente Q to act over longer timescales and solve complex, multi-step quantum chemistry tasks (discussed further in Strength 2: Scalability for long-term acting computational tasks). The agents can be broadly categorized into three functional modules -the geometry module (coral), the quantum calculation module (blue), and the file I/O module (yellow). Each module can be thought of as a department in a complex organization with its own manager, employees, and tools (violet). For example, the geometry generation agent gets to decide if the system should be handled by the organometallic complexes agent or Perplexity AI search (78), and decide the charge and multiplicity of the system.

div.head: University-level exercises
div.p: We benchmarked El Agente Q on a set of university-level exercises (79). These exercises cover three core computational categories of tasks that are time-consuming yet commonly encountered: geometry optimization, thermodynamic stability, and electronic structure analysis. To assess the capacity for autonomous problemsolving, we framed each exercise as a chemical problem rather than a direct computational instruction in our query prompts (individual query prompts provided in Supplemental note 1: Benchmark Studies). This framework was designed to evaluate its ability to reason through chemical problems and independently select appropriate computational methods and tools for each unique exercise, rather than follow fixed workflows. For example, in Exercise 5, we asked the agent to determine the pKa of carboxylic acid without explicitly asking it to compute the Gibbs free energy of the deprotonation reaction. Table 1 outlines the tasks, examples of tested systems, and the anticipated challenges associated with each task. All our evaluations are run in fully autonomous mode, with only one input from the user, although in practical use cases, El Agente Q can be highly interactive at all hierarchies.
Table 1 Summary of university-level exercises, including the task description, some examples of tested chemical systems, and challenges expected.

div.head: Organic compounds
div.p: Task: Optimize molecules from chemical names and generate a report of: geometry, point group symmetry, dipole moment, molecular orbital analysis, HOMO-LUMO gap, various atomic charges, and a visualized image of the molecule.

div.head: Systems:
div.p: The test set includes acetaminophen, 2-chloronitrobenzene, (S)-2-ethyl-2-fluoropentan-1-ol, reliability. The success rate is defined as the percentage of successful runs out of these 10 trials (the rubrics for each exercise can be found in Table S8, while all generated files can be found in a data repository (80)). Across all university-level exercises, El Agente Q achieved an average success rate of >88.8% and >87.6% for first-and second-level difficulties, respectively, demonstrating strong generalization across a wide diversity of chemical problems (Table 2). These results highlight its potential as a reliable quantum chemistry assistant that can reason through varied chemical queries, plan and execute appropriate computational workflows, and adapt to varied input file formats and job execution requirements. We further investigate the sources of performance variability across runs in the Limitations section. These failure modes, in turn, will help us inform the immediate development plans (see El Agente's Roadmap).

Table 2 Success rates of El Agente Q tested on university-level quantum chemistry exercises. The success rate is defined as the percentage of successful runs out of the total number of runs (10), with standard deviation indicated with ±. The difficulty levels are described in the table. The number of molecules (provided as SMILES or in XYZ format) involved in some tasks is given in parentheses. For the detailed score of each session, refer to Table S3.

div.head: Adaptive troubleshooting and error handling
div.p: El Agente Q demonstrates robust in situ debugging and adaptive error recovery during workflow execution, actively iterating to correct both input file issues and output-related failures. When input file errors arise, the agent can detect and correct non-executable or invalid job configurations by routing feedback through the agent hierarchy and retrying job submission (Figure 3). For example, in the calculation of absorption spectra of organic molecules (Exercise 6), El Agente Q successfully resolved ORCA runtime errors triggered by hallucinated non-existent ORCA keywords such as DOSINGLET, DOTRIPLET, and NROOTS_TRIPLET, autonomously removing or replacing them (Session TDDFTforS1andT1_level2_10). In another case, the agent initially failed to specify the correct XYZ input file for one of the runs in the pKa exercise (Exercise 5), which caused errors during batch submission (Session pKaOfCarboxylicAcidsAndMethods_level2_-3). El Agente Q automatically recovered from this error and adapted its strategy by switching to a one-at-a-time submission strategy. These examples highlight the agent's adaptive troubleshooting capacity and ability to refine its computational plan in response to failed or invalid configurations. They also demonstrate the network's internal critic mechanism, enabled by its hierarchical design. Regarding output troubleshooting, El Agente Q can handle undesirable behaviours such as the presence of imaginary frequencies. For instance, in the ring strain exercise (Exercise 4), when structure generation tools produced a planar geometry instead of the correct puckered conformation for cyclobutane, the imaginary frequency removal module accurately diagnosed the presence of imaginary frequencies, identified the underlying structural issue, and triggered re-runs by displacing the structure along the displacement modes to successfully re-optimize to the true minimum-energy structure (Session RingStrainEnergies_level2_9. In the carbocation exercise (Exercise 3), we also consistently observed the automatic correction of imaginary frequencies for several carbocation structures (i.e., the carbocation of propane and 2-methylpropane). Additionally, we observe that El Agente Q actively iterates to debug and resolve energy convergence issues during geometry optimizations (Session OrganicMoleculesGeometryOptimizationAndProperties_level1_4).

div.head: From Theory to Practice-El Agente Q in Real-World Scenarios
div.p: In this section, we evaluate El Agente Q's ability to tackle computational tasks of increased complexity through two case studies. In the first one, El Agente Q is tasked with investigating how water as a solvent affects an amino acid's IR spectrum using both implicit and explicit models. In the second, it is asked to perform the automated generation and optimization of a lanthanoid complex, guided by details from a published computational methodology. These examples highlight the model's robustness and relevance for real-world scientific applications.

div.head: Case study 1: Influence of Solvent on IR Spectra
div.p: In this study, we evaluated El Agente Q's capability to model solvent effects on vibrational spectra-a nuanced and computation-intensive task in theoretical chemistry. The exercise was adapted from a YouTube tutorial (81), and involved calculating the vibrational frequencies of alanine in three distinct environments:

(1) the gas phase, (2) implicit solvation using the CPCM model (82) with water, and (3) explicit solvation with 12 water molecules combined with CPCM. El Agente Q was expected to generate molecular geometries, prepare accurate input files using DFT, and extract key vibrational frequencies (C --O and O -H stretches) to assess solvent-induced shifts.

El Agente Q performed effectively across all stages. It successfully built the complex alanine-water cluster via OpenBabel, pre-optimized the structure with xTB, and performed geometry optimization and frequency analysis using the requested level of theory. Interestingly, El Agente Q allocated 8, 16, and 24 cores to the gas-phase, CPCM, and explicit-CPCM hybrid models, respectively, reflecting an awareness of the increasing system complexity. This behaviour indicates El Agente Q's ability to allocate computational resources efficiently within the limits of a 48-core node, and optimize parallel performance. The extracted vibrational frequencies closely approach reference values from the benchmark (81), indicating that the overall computational workflow was reliably reproduced. Impressively, El Agente Q also automatically generated a comparative IR spectrum combining results from the aforementioned calculation models, with visually highlighted characteristic absorption bands, including 1770-1850 cm -1 (C --O stretching region), 2800-3100 cm -1 (C -H stretching modes), and 3300-3800 cm -1 (N -H and O -H stretching region) (see SI: Influence of solvent on IR Spectra). Since El Agente Q assigned peaks in the spectrum based on characteristic frequency ranges, the significantly red-shifted O -H stretching peak of alanine in the hybrid solvation model (2991 cm -1 ) was grouped within the C -H stretching region, and the O -H stretching vibrations from both alanine and water molecules were classified into a single group. Nevertheless, our system reproduced the key qualitative trend-a red shift in both C --O and O -H stretches due to solvation-with clear reasoning linked to hydrogen bonding effects, demonstrating both technical reliability and chemical insight.

div.head: Case study 2: Lanthanoid Complex
div.p: In general, lanthanoid complexes present a significant challenge in computational chemistry due to their intricate electronic structures, frequent open-shell character, and the necessity of using effective core potentials. As such, accurate modelling of their properties often demands specialized methods and careful control over convergence settings. In this study, we evaluate El Agente Q's ability to autonomously carry out a highfidelity quantum chemical workflow on a Ce(III) complex containing three bidentate nitrate ligands and three coordinated water molecules. We also assess its capacity to extract and apply methodological details from the literature by prompting it with the computational procedure used to generate the Ln-QM dataset, as reported by Hölzer et al. (83) (exactly as it was described in the manuscript, see SI: Lanthanoid Complex). Although the protocol was provided in a single prompt, it required El Agente Q to execute a series of interdependent steps.

As a first step, El Agente Q utilized the Architector library (74) to generate initial geometries, showcasing its ability to integrate with community-developed tools for building organometallic structures. As the Architector library is likely not part of the training corpus of the LLMs, we developed a metal complex generation agent to call Architector's functions appropriately, which is called by the geometry generation agent (Figure 2). After successfully generating five geometrical isomers, it optimized each, ensuring consistent treatment across all calculations. During the DFT calculations, the system autonomously corrected, through iterative refinement, several input-related errors that were encountered, such as the misplacement of SCF keywords and unsupported density functional options.

For this study, geometry optimizations converged for all isomers, and two cases involving imaginary frequencies were handled appropriately: both were re-optimized until the imaginary frequencies were eliminated entirely up to a threshold of 15 cm -1 . Although geometry optimization was conducted using dispersion-corrected DFT, only the DFT energies were reported, but the energies associated with the dispersion corrections were not extracted. Nevertheless, the final single-point energies calculated using a different functional and the corresponding relative energies for the isomers were computed and reported correctly.

This case study demonstrates El Agente Q's ability to extract computational workflows from the literature to perform high-throughput quantum chemical calculations involving f -block systems-a capability readily extendable to a broad range of metal complexes. This study is an example of El Agente Q's capacity to carry out calculations with minimal human intervention, combining intelligent error handling with seamless integration of external tools for molecular structure generation and simulation. Moving forward, El Agente Q will be further refined to incorporate chemical intuition for selecting more accurate methods, including appropriate treatments of effective core potentials, spin-orbit coupling, and SCF (internal) stability checks. We anticipate that its troubleshooting capabilities will support the reliable convergence of complexes with increasingly challenging electronic wavefunctions. Data extraction failures, such as the omission of DFT dispersion data extraction in this run, will be corrected in future versions with more specialized and robust extraction modules and scripting tools.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We will begin this section by describing three strengths of El Agente before discussing its limitations and our future roadmap. We end this section with the conclusion about our study.

div.head: Strength 1: Potential to synthesize workflows
div.p: El Agente Q can automatically design workflows to achieve a specified scientific target. Within each workflow, there are decision-making and action steps. The agentic nature of our system enables it to make decisions dynamically, exploring different action sequences following best domain practices to achieve the desired objective(s). Once these action sequences are consolidated-by removing the often present trial-and-error steps-they can be reused as rigid workflows without agentic decision-making, for example, for applying them to high-throughput settings. Therefore, El Agente Q's task execution can be viewed as a search over the space of potential computational workflows. The six benchmark exercises involved an average of 64.5 actions and 103.9 agent interactions (commanding and reporting) per exercise (Tables S4, S5), demonstrating the complexity of the synthesized workflows. This capability enables efficient discovery of feasible workflows for high-throughput tasks and the reproduction of experiments from loosely defined instructions, with the potential to significantly reduce human workload by accommodating software-specific input requirements and uncovering missing details that typically require intensive tuning.

div.head: Strength 2: Scalability for long-term acting computational tasks
div.p: Another key strength of El Agente Q is its capacity to operate as a long-term autonomous system, capable of executing extended, multi-step tasks that involve numerous calculations, tool calls, and iterative decisionmaking in our benchmark exercises. The hierarchical task decomposition in our system architecture enables this long-term acting capability. Instead of requiring a single agent to reason and complete the task within its context window, our underlying architecture decomposes the complex task into smaller, manageable subtasks, each assigned to specialized agents. This assignment happens recursively until it reaches the bottom layer of the network.

In our design, the maximum depth from the computational chemist to the lowest level agent is six, which means that at some step, the low-level agent is processing a subtask that is decomposed six times from the main objective. This modular, hierarchical structure enables the overall system to maintain coherence and continuity even as the total task context exceeds the native token limits of any individual model. For example, for the RelativeStabilitiesOfCarbocations_level2_1 session, El Agente Q spends 3.2 million total tokens and 112 actions. By the end of the session, the final context length summed across all agents reached 204,789 tokens, which exceeds Claude 3.7's 200K window for a single agent. Due to the hierarchy in our framework, the computational chemist, our highest level agent, only consumes 19,855 tokens during the entire task, which is just 10% of the maximum context window (Tables S6, S7). Consequently, El Agente Q can continually function well after this task due to the low cognitive load. Its hierarchical working memory management, adaptive troubleshooting, and error handling capacity are crucial for scaling El Agente Q to more complex quantum chemistry workflows.

div.head: Strength 3: Efficiency and user accessibility
div.p: El Agente Q is a user-friendly tool that requires only a natural language prompt to define the compounds and reactions, and state the type of calculations required. By lowering the knowledge barrier for planning computational workflows and using computational chemistry and cheminformatics packages, El Agente Q makes these calculations more accessible to a much broader set of practitioners, including students or experimental research chemists with no programming knowledge. At the same time, El Agente Q's ability to export full action traces ensures transparency and traceability by allowing users to review the agents' decisionmaking process and validate the outcomes. This feature improves trust in El Agente Q's results. Additionally, El Agente Q significantly saves human time by automating tedious steps, such as the preprocessing of input files, setting up calculation parameters, and managing the job queue according to the progress of the calculations and computation resources.

div.head: Strength 4: Orthogonality to model capability and reasoning frameworks
div.p: El Agente cognitive architecture is orthogonal to the underlying LLM's capability and the external reasoning frameworks applied during inference. Improvements in model capability, such as stronger priors or fine-tuning, and reasoning strategies like chain-of-thought prompting (84) or voting-based methods (e.g., Tree of Thoughts (85)) can enhance the quality of local decision-making and instruction following at the node level. For instance, during initial system development, we observed higher performance gains after switching from non-reasoning models to reasoning-capable models like Claude 3.7, particularly in tasks requiring the model to reason with given context. El Agente complements these model improvements by leveraging its hierarchical structure to reduce cognitive load at each expert node, allowing the reasoning core to focus on the most relevant context, enabling both the model and the applied reasoning framework to perform closer to their optimal potential.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: While El Agente Q demonstrates strong overall performance, we discuss some sources of performance variability that we observed (Table 2).

First, one issue is incomplete or missing final reports and/or property extractions during post-computation analysis, particularly for larger parallel batches of longer calculations. For example, in the geometry optimization of organic compounds (Exercise 1), none of the first-level calculations reports were missing, while 24.5% (49 out of 200) of the reports for second-level calculations were missing. In the case of inorganic compounds (Exercise 2), only 1.3% (2 out of 160) of the reports for second-level calculations were missing, and this was due to issues encountered while optimizing the XeF 4 geometry. Calculations for the organic molecules required significantly longer runtimes when compared to inorganic molecules, with most compounds containing about 20 atoms. Among the reports generated for Exercises 1 and 2, El Agente Q was also penalized for not including one or two requested properties in the final report. This penalization was the primary factor contributing to the scores presented in Table 2, as we applied strict scoring criteria. Importantly, we found that this issue is resolved by issuing a simple follow-up query prompt to generate the analysis reports after completing the calculations. This finding highlights that the failure did not stem from an inability to perform the calculations and their corresponding analyses, and that El Agente Q could benefit from an additional dedicated post-analysis module integrated into the existing hierarchy, and better output file parsing tools.

Another source of performance variability is the model's tendency to make unverified assumptions if the provided information is incomplete. For instance, in the pKa benchmark exercise (Exercise 5), the model directly applied empirical corrections using arbitrary scaling values to adjust computed pKa values (Session pKaOfCar-boxylicAcidsAndMethods_level1_6). In one of the runs on the relative stabilities of carbocations (Exercise 3), following an incorrect/missing calculation for the enthalpy and Gibbs energies of the hydride anion, the agent approximated the enthalpy as -0.5 Hartree based on the statistical mechanics of an ideal gas, instead of resubmitting the DFT calculation at the specified level of theory (Session RelativeStabilitiesOfCarboca-tions_level2_4). Nonetheless, traceability and interpretability are preserved through our detailed action trace logs and conversation history that capture all model decisions, allowing users to catch these assumptions. Future improvements, such as more interactive clarification prompts and multimodal verification strategies, are outlined in El Agente's Roadmap and will further enhance output reliability while balancing user oversight and system autonomy. These behaviours could also be mitigated through alternative prompting strategies, such as explicitly instructing the agent to refrain from making assumptions, or adjusting the model's prior, such as through reinforcement learning from human feedback (86).

A further limitation lies in the reliability of geometry generation from compound names or SMILES strings. The external tools to which El Agente Q has current access (e.g., OpenBabel or RDKit) do not always generate conformationally stable or chemically reasonable structures. This constraint arises from the inherent limitations of the current geometry generation tools rather than the agentic framework. An interactive mode, where the users can inspect, draw, or modify the generated structures before El Agente Q proceeds, can potentially mitigate this issue. The interactive format inherently comes with a trade-off on the system's autonomy. Expanding El Agente Q's access to more diverse structure generation tools with multimodal capabilities could also enhance reliability. Plans to implement these system upgrades are detailed in El Agente's Roadmap.

Additionally, the system architecture involved careful manual design of the agent hierarchy to address early multi-agent coordination failures (87), taking into account the tools' availability and model limitations. For instance, when we experimented with lightweight LLMs during early development stages of El Agente Q, without specifying explicit constraints, the geometry optimization agent might proceed in the absence of a valid initial geometry. Other failure modes, such as loss of details during message passing, also required further tuning of the message passing and global memory construction policies. These experiences highlight the need for robust orchestration strategies, such as internal validation and pre-condition checks, to ensure reliable behaviour across models with varying capabilities. These safeguards will be critical for scaling under resource constraints, e.g., when one desires to employ lightweight LLMs. A promising direction is to allow El Agente Q to learn and adopt these safeguards autonomously through its episodic memory.

Despite these challenges, El Agente Q represents a promising step toward automating traditionally manual and expertise-heavy aspects of computational chemistry, such as recovering from execution errors or generating input files for unfamiliar software packages. With the continued development of both infrastructure and domain-specific capabilities, El Agente Q holds substantial potential to advance autonomy in scientific workflows. Looking ahead, integrating Model Context Protocol (MCP) (88) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) (89) communication could further enrich its interoperability with other agentic systems.

div.head: El Agente's Roadmap
div.p: We will release a cloud-enabled alpha version of El Agente Q in the https://elagente.ca website as the immediate next step for the users to be able to employ the tool (Stage 1). Beyond that, a critical step in the future development of El Agente Q is expanding the range of accessible calculations, from molecular properties to advanced computational simulations, as shown in Building on this foundation, we plan to generalize El Agente Q's framework to operate across a variety of molecular quantum chemistry software platforms, such as Q-Chem (99), Gaussian (100), OpenMolcas (101), PySCF (102), and others (103; 104) (Stage 4). To further broaden its scope, El Agente Q will be adapted for applications in solid-state chemistry and materials science (Stage 5). These applications require support for periodic boundary condition calculations and integration with software packages specialized in crystalline and heterogeneous phase materials, such as Quantum ESPRESSO (105), VASP (106), Abinit (107), and NWChem (108). This extension would open the door to studying materials for catalysis, energy storage, and semiconductor applications within the same agentic framework. This generalization will extend compatibility to GPU-accelerated software (109) and enable the automated generation of high-throughput screening scripts, thereby facilitating large-scale computational studies across different codes and hardware environments (Stage 6).

Another critical milestone for El Agente Q's roadmap is the integration of machine learning (ML) tools (Stage 7) at different points in the workflow to further enhance the computational abilities of the agent (110). Prediction models can be used for adaptive experimentation, such as in active learning or Bayesian optimization (111; 112; 113), or extend computational results by acting as a proxy that can extrapolate to new data points and provide faster predictions (114; 115; 116; 117; 118; 119). Advanced ML models can be used to enhance quantum chemical calculations directly, such as in machine learned force fields (120; 121; 122), or neural wavefunctions (123; 124). Furthermore, ML generative models can be used for ideation and generation of experiments, such as in the inverse-design of materials and molecules (125). By incorporating ML tools such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) (126; 127; 128), flow-based models (129; 130), diffusion models (131), and language models (132; 133; 134; 135), El Agente Q would be capable of generating novel materials and compounds conditioned on properties of interest, allowing it to produce higher-level hypotheses for subsequent testing and exploration. Benchmarking tasks that have been established for chemical generative models can also be incorporated into the tool set of El Agente Q, some of which are built from the quantum chemistry capabilities in earlier milestones (136; 137; 138; 139; 140). Finally, El Agente Q can be augmented with the ability to train its own ML models. Combining training with its ability to curate its own data from quantum chemistry would enable El Agente Q to continually improve its tools.

div.head: A further crucial extension involves molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (Stage 8).
div.p: El Agente Q will thus implement enhanced sampling techniques such as metadynamics, free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations, Grand-Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC), hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) simulations, and ab initio MD, thereby enabling the study of rare events, reaction free energies, and complex systems with improved accuracy and efficiency. Therefore, the integration of standard MD packages, such as OpenMM (141), GROMACS (142), LAMMPS (143), RASPA (144), and CP2K (145), along with providing functionality to extract relevant physical properties from MD trajectories, would enable El Agente Q to study the time-dependent and temperature-dependent behaviours of molecules and materials.

Specialized workflows will be developed to expand El Agente Q's applicability across key research areas (Stage 9), including but not limited to catalysis, materials science, drug discovery, solar energy conversion, and batteries. By customizing the agents' capabilities to meet the specific demands of these fields, El Agente Q will be better equipped to tackle complex, domain-specific challenges and drive innovation across a broad range of scientific applications.

The last milestone in our roadmap (Stage 10) envisions the integration of El Agente Q with self-driving labs (SDLs) (146) by "agentifying" an SDL's core functional components, including the librarian, executer, planner, and coordinator (147). For example, the librarian component can leverage data mining frameworks (148; 149; 150) to extract reactions and chemical data from literature and analyze them using computational workflows, while ensuring interoperability by connecting to cloud-based and community-curated databases (151; 152; 153; 154) and aligning with FAIR data principles (155). A central challenge is the need for a shared executable ontology to unify data exchange, which remains an active field of research (156; 157; 154). The El Agente Q system can support the executor component to verify the safety and validity of the proposed experiments and literature-derived inputs (158; 159; 160), such as through quantum chemistry-informed reaction safety screening (158). Integration with the planner could enable agent-led Bayesian optimization using both computational and experimental data to further enhance the efficiency of exploratory workflows (161; 162; 163; 164; 165; 166; 167). Lastly, realizing the vision of distributed, autonomous discovery across globally connected SDLs (168; 156; 169; 170; 171) requires coordination via robust operating systems. An agentic SDL approach centred on modular, communicative, and semantically grounded agents can offer a unifying abstraction layer across different operating systems and workflow management frameworks (172; 173; 174; 175; 147; 176; 177), improving standardization and interoperability (178; 179; 180).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we introduced an agent system capable of understanding and executing quantum chemistry tasks with a high degree of success. We also demonstrate the agentic architecture's ability to generalize to new problems that it has not been previously taught to do and successfully simulate a lanthanoid complex and an IR spectrum. Furthermore, its ability to visualize the molecule and export the action traces allows for human expert inspection and expedites building workflows for virtual high-throughput screening. These capabilities pave the way to more accessible and less time-consuming computational chemistry tasks.

We envisage that in the future, building and running computational chemistry calculations will be completely autonomous and high-level. LLM-based agents are only expected to become cheaper and smarter. Progress on the science of agent systems can also be easily ported into our system. Scientists will focus on the scientific problems at hand, providing high-level strategic thinking without spending time writing scripts and handling exceptions. These advancements can democratize computational chemistry, enabling deeper, more autonomous scientific development.

div.head: El Agente Infrastructure
div.p: Our LLM-based multi-agent system was implemented with a combination of off-the-shelf and custom components. LangGraph (v0.2.74) and LangChain (v0.3.19) were used to manage single-agent orchestration, including tool use and memory management, due to their simplicity and flexibility in defining diverse agent behaviours. The specific LLM model used for each agent, OpenAI's gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 and Anthropic's claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, is detailed in the Supporting Information Table S1, with model selection guided by empirical performance. The overarching multi-agent coordination, including task delegation, state sharing, and interaction logic, was implemented through custom logic external to LangGraph, providing fine-grained control over agent collaboration.

Each agent was initialized with a specialized context and task-specific semantic memory, further refined through human experts' interactive instruction during system development. The episodic memory of each agent, capturing interaction histories and state transitions, was recorded in a MongoDB backend for provenance tracking and retrospective analysis. The global memory was implemented as a session-specific shared file storing contents accessible to all agents. The content is also dynamically generated and edited by agents. This mechanism mitigates potential information loss in message passing during long-horizon, multi-agent workflows.

div.head: Human Teaching
div.p: Adapting the agentic system for this particular problem required vast expert-human time. The effort was two-fold: first, human subject matter experts were necessary to teach the agents the standard procedures of running quantum chemistry software packages. These procedures include running geometry optimization before obtaining the energy differences, or running frequency calculation after geometry optimization to ensure the optimization lands on a minimum. This teaching was implemented by augmenting each agent's semantic memory and initialization procedural context with curated domain knowledge and annotated examples. The second part of the effort was to give the agent a list of allowed commands in the keyword line or each of the input file blocks of ORCA, so that it compares against the allowed list. This process is tedious, yet necessary to ensure that the agent does not hallucinate and generate incorrect input files.

div.head: Generation of Agent Context Files for ORCA Input Blocks
div.p: To support automated generation of ORCA input files, we constructed a suite of structured, markdownformatted context files-each describing the syntax, function, and decision logic for a specific ORCA input block or keyword type (e.g., %method, %scf, %geom, %tddft, etc.). These files serve as internal context for keyword-line related experts, such as runtype expert, configuration recommender, and nine block experts managed by input file expert, guiding it in synthesizing complete and reliable input files that follow good domain practice. A complementary strategy that fine-tunes an LLM to emit full ORCA inputs in a single pass was recently described by Jacobs and Pollice (32), while our approach utilizes hierarchy agents and in-context learning to facilitate correct and sophisticated input file synthesis.
Each context file follows a consistent structure:
• Introduction: Brief description of the block and its role in an ORCA calculation.
• Interaction with Upstream Agent: Specifies when the block should be triggered based on the keyword line or system characteristics.
• Mandatory Requirement: States whether the block is always required, optional, or conditionally generated.
• Key Parameters Table : Summarizes the most relevant options, default values (if applicable), and their meaning.
• Usage Notes: Provides practical recommendations and interpretation of the settings.
• Exclusion Criteria: Specifies when the block should not be included.
• Final Considerations: Summarizes best practices and pitfalls to avoid.

File Generation Process Each input file is generated by the input file expert, who consults related experts to determine the partial contents of the input file. For example, the input file expert can ask the %pal block expert to generate the parallelization block that specifies the number of cores. The %pal block expert will evaluate the system size and number of cores available in the HPC Cluster to determine the optimal settings for the calculation. The recommended settings will be assembled with other recommendations by the input file expert and saved as an input file.

Consistent with the generate-then-verify paradigm proven effective in the CLAIRify framework for chemistry-robotics planning (181), syntax or configuration errors can be corrected with ORCA's error feedback after job submission, allowing dynamic error recovery and exception handling.

div.head: Computational Tools
div.p: El Agente Q is enabled by many specialized agents and tools, each with a specific functionality (Tables S1, S2). Below is a list of the main tools employed in the system, along with their respective roles:

1. Python: The agentic framework is implemented in Python (v3.11.11), which serves as the primary interface programming language for all agents and tools. Furthermore, Python is used to perform I/O operations and analysis.

2. Shell: File manipulation and job submission to the SLURM scheduler are performed using shell commands, executed within Python. All experiments were conducted on the HPC cluster running Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS. 3. SLURM: The SLURM scheduler (v23.11.10) is used to manage job submission and execution on the HPC cluster. 4. OpenBabel: OpenBabel (v3.1.0) is used to generate molecular geometries from SMILES strings, especially for organic molecules. 5. RDKit: RDKit (v2024.09.5) is used to generate molecular geometries from SMILES strings, especially for inorganic compounds. 6. Architector: Architector (v0.0.10) is used to generate molecular geometries for organometallic complexes. 7. ORCA: ORCA (v6.0.1) is the main quantum chemistry software used for all calculations. 8. xTB: The xTB (v6.7.1) package is used for fast geometry optimization between OpenBabel/RDKitgenerated geometries and ORCA.

div.head: Graphical User Interface
div.p: To facilitate seamless interaction between users and El Agente Q, the graphical user interface (GUI) web-based platform was developed using the Python Flask framework (v3.1.0) in combination with Uvicorn (v0.32.1) as the ASGI server. The core functionality of the GUI is a chat interface designed to enable users to send and receive messages from the nodes of the multi-agent system in real-time. This interaction was established through MongoDB using the PyMongo package (v4.6.1) for database communication and Pydantic (v2.10.3) for data validation and schema enforcement. Each agent response contains interaction content and also includes annotations, such as timestamps that describe the reasoning process and the tools utilized by the agents during execution. Users can direct queries to specific agent nodes and filter responses to isolate interactions with particular nodes, which supports fine-grained control over multi-agent coordination. The system also incorporates comprehensive session management, allowing users to initiate and switch between different sessions, as well as to export entire session workflows into Jupyter notebooks for reproducibility and further analysis. Additional features such as pausing and resuming conversations at breakpoints, clearing chat histories, and managing uploaded images enhance usability and support long-term engagement with complex workflows. It should be noted that each university-level exercise and case study presented in this paper was invoked by only a single user query to the computational_chemist agent. The interactive chat was mainly used during system development for human teaching.

In addition to the chat interface, several advanced features have been integrated into the GUI to extend its capabilities. Firstly, the graph visualization tool, built with the vis-network JavaScript library (v9.1.2), displays active agents and the tools they are currently using, offering real-time insight into system behavior. Secondly, a semantic memory module enables persistent and context-aware knowledge retention across sessions, improving the coherence and adaptability of the El Agente Q over time. A file browser has been implemented and equipped with support for molecule visualization, allowing users to explore structured data, artifacts, and output files produced or consumed by the agents during execution. Together, these components form an integrated interface for managing, observing, and directing multi-agent workflows in El Agente Q.

div.head: Ring Strain Energies of Cycloalkanes Introduction
div.p: This report presents the calculated ring strain energies for cycloalkanes from n=3 to n=8, based on the reaction energies for the conversion: cyclo(CnH2n) → cyclo(Cn-1H2n-3)-CH3. All calculations were performed at the B3LYP/6-31G(d) level of theory with full geometry optimization and frequency calculations.

div.head: Computational Methods
div.p: • All structures were optimized using B3LYP/6-31G(d) with frequency calculations • Ring strain energies were calculated using isodesmic reactions • Two reference points were considered: cyclooctane (n=8) and cyclohexane (n=6)

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The computed ring strain energies show the expected trend for cycloalkanes:

1. Cyclohexane has the lowest strain energy when using cyclooctane as reference 2. Cyclopropane and cyclobutane show the highest strain energies due to their highly strained structures 3. When using cyclohexane as reference (which is often considered strain-free experimentally), the calculated strain energies align well with experimental trends The trend reflects the well-known ring strain patterns of cycloalkanes where: -Small rings (n=3,4) have high angle strain -Medium rings (n=5,6) have less strain -Larger rings (n=7,8) show increasing strain due to transannular interactions
The calculated energies support cyclohexane's special stability with its strain-free chair conformation, as indicated by its minimum strain value in the cyclooctane-referenced results.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The computed ring strain energies using DFT calculations (B3LYP/6-31G(d)) provide a good model for understanding the relative stability of cycloalkanes. The results demonstrate that cyclohexane has the lowest strain energy, confirming its special stability observed experimentally. The trend of ring strain energies across the cycloalkane series follows the expected pattern based on molecular structure considerations.
Note: All calculations were performed using ORCA with the B3LYP/6-31G(d) level of theory. The enthalpy and Gibbs free energy values were obtained from frequency calculations at 298.15 K.

div.head: Analysis
div.p: The calculated pKa value of -2.40 for chlorofluoroacetic acid indicates that it is a significantly stronger acid than both fluoroacetic acid (pKa = 2.586) and chloroacetic acid (pKa = 2.86). This result demonstrates the strong electron-withdrawing effects of having both chlorine and fluorine substituents on the same carbon atom, which stabilize the conjugate base to a greater extent than either substituent alone. The very low (negative) pKa value suggests that chlorofluoroacetic acid is a superacid that completely dissociates in water. The combined electron-withdrawing effects of both halogen substituents severely weaken the O-H bond in the carboxylic acid group, leading to extremely easy deprotonation. The variation in predicted pKa values depending on which reference acid is used (-4.77 to -0.08) indicates some uncertainty in the calculation, but all predictions consistently show that chlorofluoroacetic acid is much more acidic than its mono-substituted counterparts.

div.head: Summary of Solvent Effects on Alanine Vibrational Frequencies
Study Overview
div.p: We successfully investigated how different solvation models affect the vibrational frequencies of alanine using DFT calculations at the PBE0/def2-TZVP level of theory. Three different environments were modeled: 1. Gas phase (no solvent) 2. Implicit solvent (CPCM water model) 3. Explicit solvent (12 water molecules + CPCM)

Key Findings 1. System Size Comparison: • Gas phase system: 33 vibrational modes • CPCM implicit solvent: 33 vibrational modes • Explicit solvent (12 H 2 O + CPCM): 141 vibrational modes 2. Solvent Effects on Key Vibrational Modes:
• N-H and O-H Stretching Region (3300-3800 cm -¹):

-Significant red shifts (lower frequencies) observed in both solvation models -Explicit solvent model showed more pronounced shifts due to direct hydrogen bonding • C=O Stretching Region (1700-1850 cm -¹):

-The carbonyl stretching frequency was highly sensitive to solvation -Both implicit and explicit solvation caused red shifts, with explicit model showing larger effects • C-H Stretching Modes (2800-3100 cm -¹):
-Less affected by solvation as C-H bonds don't typically form hydrogen bonds with water 3. Comparison of Solvation Models:

• The CPCM implicit model captured general solvent effects but missed specific directional interactions • The explicit solvent model provided a more realistic representation of the solvation environment, particularly for functional groups involved in hydrogen bonding

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This study demonstrates that: 1. Solvent environments significantly impact the vibrational frequencies of alanine, especially for groups capable of hydrogen bonding 2. The magnitude of frequency shifts correlates with the strength of hydrogen bonding interactions 3. The hybrid approach of combining explicit water molecules with a continuum model offers a balanced compromise between computational efficiency and accurate representation of solvation effects All results have been documented in detail in the comprehensive report located at alanine\_-spectrum\_analysis/alanine\_solvation\_report.md, along with comparative IR spectra plots showing the differences between the three environments.

Figure S2 Comparative IR spectra generated by El Agente Q for the alanine system in three different environments, with visually highlighted frequency regions corresponding to key vibrational modes. The red, green, and blue lines represent the spectra for the gas-phase model, the CPCM model with water, and the explicit solvation with 12 water molecules combined with CPCM, respectively. The plot was automatically generated by the agent using repl_tool, where matplotlib codes were created and executed as part of the agent's post-processing workflow.

In accordance with general recommendations on the selection of DFT functionals,57 single-point feature calculations have been conducted using the range-separated hybrid ωB97M-V functional48,49 utilizing the def2-SVPD basis. 52-54 This functional integrates the post-SCF evaluated VV10 nonlocal dispersion correction.58 For feature calculation, TightSCF convergence criteria were used. The basis set was chosen to be efficient due to the large number of calculations required for the data set, while also accommodating for anions via the diffuse functions. The def2-ECP Effective Core Potentials (ECPs) were employed for the lanthanoids. Make sure the scf autotrah setting is off for both geometry optimization and single point calculation. Make sure to use 16 cores for each calculation. Also make sure the convergence max iteration for both opt and scf should be at least 500. Lanthanides are known to not easy to converge. figure.head: Figure 3
figure.figDesc: Figure 3 Hierarchical architecture of El Agente Q. Inter-agent communication is illustrated with black arrows, where solid arrows represent task delegation from higher-level agents, and dotted arrows indicate feedback and reporting from lower-level agents.The agents can be broadly categorized into three functional modules -the geometry module (coral), the quantum calculation module (blue), and the file I/O module (yellow). Each module can be thought of as a department in a complex organization with its own manager, employees, and tools (violet). For example, the geometry generation agent gets to decide if the system should be handled by the organometallic complexes agent or Perplexity AI search (78), and decide the charge and multiplicity of the system.

figure.head: Figure 4 .
figure.figDesc: This expansion includes the incorporation of user-friendly interfaces-such as enabling users to draw and manipulate molecular structures directly, similar to the functionality provided by tools like JMol (90; 91), ChemDoodle (92), and ChemDraw (93)-thereby making the system more flexible and accessible to a broader range of academic and industrial researchers (Stage 2). Another key development in the initial stage of El Agente Q will be the expansion of its current toolkit to include spectroscopic property predictions, reaction mechanisms, photochemical processes, and high-level single-and multi-reference electronic structure methods as well as excited state methods, such as DLPNO-CCSD(T) (94), MC-PDFT (95), ADC(2) (96; 97) and NEVPT2 (98) (Stage 3).

figure.head: Figure 4
figure.figDesc: Figure 4 El Agente Q Development Roadmap: Bridging Molecular Properties, Advanced Simulations, and Self-Driving Lab Integration. The milestones are not drawn to timescale.

div.head: Ring Strain Analysis of Cycloalkanes via Reaction Energies Introduction
div.p: Ring strain is a major factor governing the stability and reactivity of cycloalkanes. In this study, we estimate relative ring strain energies of cyclopropane through cyclooctane by computing reaction enthalpies (∆H) and free energies (∆G) for the formal transformation cyclo-(C n H 2n ) → methylcyclo-(C n-1 H 2n-3 ) using B3LYP/6-31G(d) enthalpies and free energies. Cyclohexane is taken as a zero-strain reference.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: • Energies (enthalpy H and Gibbs free energy G) in hartree were obtained from DFT frequency calculations at B3LYP/6-31G(d).
• Reaction energies ∆H and ∆G (hartree) converted to kcal/mol by multiplying with 1 hartree = 627.5095 kcal/mol.
• Reaction ∆(n) = H(methylcyclo (n-1) ) -H(cyclo n ) (and similarly for G) approximates the difference in ring strain between the n-membered ring and the (n-1)-membered ring.

• Cyclohexane (n=6) strain is set to zero. Ring strain for n<6 accumulated downward via strain(n-1) = ∆H(n) + strain(n) and for n>6 upward via strain(n) = strain(n-1) -∆H(n). Let me organize the report files into a dedicated folder:
Tool used:

Tool Name: interact_with_os_and_files Arguments: message2agent: Please create a folder named "results" and move the report.md file and ring_strain_-vs_size.png (if it exists) into that folder. Let me also create a simple visualization of the optimized geometries to include with our report:

Tool Name: geometry_visualization Arguments: message2agent: Please create visualizations of all the optimized geometries for the cycloalkanes (cyclopropane to cyclooctane) and display them side by side in order from smallest to largest ring size. Use ball-and-stick representation and clearly show the ring structure. The optimized geometries should be found in their respective optimization folders. Save this visualization to the results folder. Tool Name: update_global_memory Arguments: log_content: Completed calculation of ring strain energies for cycloalkanes (n=3-8) using B3LYP/6-31G(d) level of theory. Analyzed reaction energies for cyclo(CnH2n) → cyclo(Cn-1H2n-3)-CH3 transformations (n=4-8) and used them to estimate relative ring strain. Established cyclohexane as zero-strain reference. Found greatest strain in cyclopropane (13.86 kcal/mol) and cyclobutane (13.63 kcal/mol), negative strain for cyclopentane (-2.20 kcal/mol), and moderate strain in cycloheptane (8.13 kcal/mol) and cyclooctane (10.85 kcal/mol). Created full report with data tables, molecule visualizations, and analysis in the results folder.

I have successfully completed the geometry optimization of all five Ce complex conformers according to your specifications. Here's a detailed report of the process and final results:

div.head: Summary of Optimization Process
div.p: 1. XTB Optimization: All five conformers were initially optimized using XTB. 2. DFT Optimization: The XTB-optimized structures were then subjected to DFT optimization with frequency calculations using ORCA with PBE0/def2-SVP/D4/RIJCOSX settings. 3. Imaginary Frequency Removal: Three conformers had no imaginary frequencies after DFT optimization, while two conformers required additional optimization steps to remove imaginary frequencies.

monogr.title: Action: Summary of Ce Complex Computational Study I have successfully completed the computational study of the Ce(III) complex with 3 nitrate_bi and 3 water ligands. Here's a summary of what was accomplished: 1. Initial Geometry Generation: Generated 5 different conformers of the Ce complex with coordination number 9

Geometry Optimization: Optimized all conformers using ORCA with PBE0/def2-SVP, D4 dispersion, RIJCOSX approximation, DEFGRID2 integration grid, and def2-ECP for Ce. For conformers with imaginary frequencies, additional optimization steps were performed to obtain true minima

Single Point Calculations: Performed single point calculations on the optimized geometries using ωB97M-V/def2-SVPD with def2-ECP for Ce. All calculations used TightSCF convergence criteria, 16 cores, and a maximum of 500 SCF iterations
Energy Analysis: Extracted and analyzed energies for all conformers, identifying the most stable structure as the capped_square_antiprismatic_0 conformer
Visualization: Generated a visualization of the most stable conformer
Final Report: Created a comprehensive report detailing the energy differences between conformers in both the optimization and single point calculation levels

Key Results: -The most stable conformer is capped_square_antiprismatic_0 with other conformers having relative energies ranging from 0.10 to 2.59 kcal/mol higher. -The energetic ordering from optimization level (PBE0/def2-SVP) differs slightly from the single point calculation level (ωB97M-V/def2-SVPD), highlighting the importance of using a high-level method for final energy evaluations

biblStruct.note: All results have been organized in the Final_Report directory, containing the energy analysis report and a visualization of the most stable conformer. computational_chemist
